title: Equipment finance credit package checklist: what lenders want to see
summary: The documents lenders want in an equipment finance credit package, app-only vs full financials, why incomplete files stall, and a checklist brokers can use.
body_markdown:
Take a paving contractor, six years in business, that wants to finance a $340,000 used milling machine from a dealer. The contractor is invented for this guide, and so is every detail of the deal. You send the lender the application, two years of tax returns and the dealer’s quote.


Two days later the credit analyst writes back. Can you send year-to-date financials? The last three months of bank statements? The quote has no serial number or hours on it. When the bank statements do arrive, they show a $2,100 monthly payment to a truck lender that is not on the debt schedule, and that needs explaining too.


Each answer takes the borrower a few days. By the time the file is complete the dealer’s quote has expired, and the borrower is asking why this is taking so long. Nothing was wrong with the credit. The package was incomplete, and every gap cost a round trip.


Quick answer


A complete equipment finance credit package usually holds a signed credit application, entity documents, recent business bank statements, two to three years of business tax returns, year-end and interim financial statements, a business debt schedule, a personal financial statement and tax returns for each guarantor, and the vendor quote or invoice for the equipment.


Smaller deals are often application only and need far less. The exact list is set by each lender, so confirm it before you ask the borrower for anything.


Key takeaways


-


Every document in an equipment finance package answers one of four questions: who is borrowing, can the business pay, who stands behind the debt, and what is the lender securing.


-


Smaller deals are often application only. Above each lender’s limit, which several lenders publish at $150,000 to $250,000, expect full business and personal financials.


-


Most stalled files are not bad credit. They are a missing month, a missing schedule, a name that does not match or a loan payment that is not on the debt schedule.


-


Ask the borrower once, with the whole list, and review the file the way the analyst will before it leaves your desk.


01


## What the lender is trying to answer


A document list is easier to remember, and easier to explain to a borrower, when you know what each item is for. An equipment finance analyst reading your file is trying to answer four questions:


-


**Who is borrowing, and who owns it?** The application, the entity documents and the ownership breakdown. Lenders that are banks have to identify everyone who owns 25% or more of a business borrower, and one person who controls it.\[6\]


-


**Can the business make the payment?** Bank statements, tax returns, financial statements and the debt schedule. This is where most of the paper is.


-


**Who stands behind the debt?** Guarantors’ credit, personal financial statements and personal tax returns.


-


**What is being financed, and can the lender secure it?** The quote or invoice, the equipment’s details, and anything that affects the lender’s claim on it, such as an existing lien.


Equipment is its own collateral, which is part of why equipment deals can be documented more lightly than other business loans of the same size. But the collateral only matters if the payment fails. The first question is still whether the business can pay, and on a full-financials deal the analyst answers it by restating the borrower’s statements in the lender’s own template, a step called[financial spreading](https://www.kita.ai/blog/what-is-financial-spreading) . Every period you leave out is a column the analyst cannot fill.


02


## Application only or full financials


How much paper a deal needs depends first on its size. Many equipment lenders run an application-only tier: below a set amount they decide mainly on the application, credit, time in business and the equipment, with no tax returns or financial statements. Crest Capital and Dimension Funding both publish a $250,000 application-only limit and ask for financial statements above it.\[1,2\] Liberty Capital Group lists $150,000 on one heavy equipment program and up to $250,000 on select others.\[3\]


Those are three lenders’ published programs, not an industry rule. Limits differ by lender, equipment type and credit, and they change. Application only also does not mean nothing but the application: Liberty’s application-only files still need the equipment quote or invoice and three to four months of business bank statements.\[3\]


How equipment finance documentation usually scales with the deal Tier When it usually applies What lenders typically ask for


Application only Smaller tickets, strong credit, established business. Published limits from three lenders run from $150,000 to $250,000.\[1,2,3\] Signed application, equipment quote or invoice, and often a few months of business bank statements. No tax returns or financial statements.


Full financials Above the lender’s application-only limit, or below it when credit, time in business or the equipment raises questions.\[1,2\] Everything above, plus business and personal tax returns, year-end and interim statements, a debt schedule and personal financial statements.


Full financials, plus Larger deals, several related companies, a startup, or used and specialized equipment. Receivables and payables aging, projections, financials for affiliated companies, and more detail on the equipment and its value.


For a broker working deals of roughly $100,000 to $750,000, this line runs straight through the book. Some deals will go application only with one lender and need full financials with another. Decide which tier you are aiming at before you ask the borrower for anything, so you ask once.


03


## The credit package checklist


This is a typical list for a deal above an application-only limit, grouped by the question each item answers. Use it as a starting point and adjust it to each funding partner’s own list.


### Equipment finance credit package checklist


Full-financials file


A · Application and identity


Who is borrowing, and who owns it?


-


Signed credit application


Every guarantor signs, with consent to pull credit


-


Exact legal name, matching the state filing\[7\]


Not the trade name


-


Articles of organization or incorporation, and operating agreement or bylaws


-


Certificate of good standing from the state


-


EIN confirmation letter from the IRS


-


Ownership breakdown and owner IDs\[6\]


Everyone at 25% or more, plus one control person


B · Business cash flow


Can the business make the payment?


-


Recent business bank statements\[3\]


Often three to six months, every page


-


Business tax returns, usually two to three years


All schedules attached


-


Year-end profit and loss and balance sheet


-


Year-to-date interim profit and loss and balance sheet


-


Business debt schedule


Lender, balance, payment, maturity, collateral


-


Receivables and payables aging


On larger or working-capital-heavy deals


C · Guarantors


Who stands behind the debt?


-


Personal financial statement for each guarantor\[5\]


-


Personal tax returns, usually two years


-


Signed Form 4506-C, if the lender verifies returns with the IRS\[4\]


D · Equipment and deal


What is being financed, and can the lender secure it?


-


Vendor quote or invoice\[3\]


Make, model, year, serial or VIN, price, tax, delivery


-


For used equipment: hours or mileage, photos, condition


-


For private-party sales: bill of sale, title, payoff letter for any existing lien


-


Source of the down payment


-


Insurance agent contact, for the certificate naming the lender


-


Your cover memo: the business, the equipment, why it pays, anything unusual


A typical list for a deal above a lender’s application-only limit. Every lender sets its own requirements, so check the funding partner’s current document list before you send the borrower yours. Application-only deals usually need only the application, the quote or invoice and, often, recent bank statements.


Most of the list is self-explanatory. A few items cause more trouble than the rest.


### The debt schedule


List every business obligation: lender, original amount, current balance, monthly payment, maturity and what secures it. Then check it against the bank statements. A recurring debit to a lender, a leasing company or a daily or weekly debit from a funding provider that is not on the schedule is one of the first things an analyst looks for, and an unexplained one costs more credibility than the debt itself.


### Bank statements


Send every page of every month, for every operating account, downloaded from the bank. Missing pages, a missing month, or a most recent statement that is already two months old are among the most common follow-up requests. If the business moved banks during the period, include both accounts.


### The legal name


The lender files its lien against the borrower’s registered name as it appears in the state’s records, and a trade name alone is not enough.\[7\] So the name on the application, the entity documents, the bank account and the invoice should all agree, and if the business operates under a trade name, say so up front.


### The equipment


A quote with a price and nothing else is a common gap. The lender wants to know exactly what it is financing: make, model, year, serial number or VIN, and for used equipment the hours or mileage, condition and photos. A private-party sale adds a bill of sale, the title and a payoff letter for any lien on the machine. Soft costs such as delivery, installation and training should be broken out, because lenders treat them differently from the equipment itself.


04


## Why lenders stall or decline incomplete files


An analyst cannot weigh a credit until the file answers the four questions. Until it does, the file sits waiting for the broker, and a file that keeps raising new questions can end in a decline that has more to do with doubt than with credit. The usual reasons:


-


**Missing periods or pages.** A tax return without its schedules, a bank statement missing a page, a year-end with no interim to bring it up to date.


-


**Numbers that do not tie.** Deposits far below the revenue on the tax return, or loan payments in the bank statements that are not on the debt schedule.


-


**Names that do not match.** A different entity on the application, the bank account and the invoice, or an owner on the operating agreement who is not on the application.


-


**Stale documents.** Interim statements several months old, an old bank statement, or a vendor quote past its expiry date.


-


**Liens the file did not mention.** A lien search can turn up another lender’s blanket lien, a claim over all of the business’s assets rather than one machine,\[8\] or a tax lien. Neither always kills a deal, but both are worse found by the lender than disclosed by you.


-


**Unexplained events.** Overdrafts, returned items, a sharp drop in deposits, a late tax filing or a recent change of ownership, with no note saying why.


Notice that most of these can be found before submission. The lender will find them anyway. The difference is whether they arrive with an explanation attached or as a question that adds another week.


05


## How to package the deal and collect what is missing


The borrower is running a business, not a loan file. Every extra request costs goodwill, and the third email asking for “one more thing” is usually the one that goes unanswered. The fix is to ask for everything once, then check it yourself before the lender does.


1. 01


Pick the lender’s tier before you ask for anything


Check the target lender’s current application-only limit and document list for this equipment type and deal size, so you ask the borrower for the right package the first time.


2. 02


Send the borrower one complete list


Send every item you need in one request, with a line on why each matters and a date to return it by. Get the application, credit consent and any Form 4506-C signed in the same pass.


3. 03


Collect source documents, not summaries


Ask for bank statements downloaded from the bank, every page of every month, and complete tax returns with all schedules. Screenshots and retyped figures invite questions.


4. 04


Review the file the way the lender will


Check periods, page counts, signatures and dates. Make sure the legal name matches across the application, entity documents, bank account and invoice, and that every loan payment in the bank statements is on the debt schedule.


5. 05


Write a short cover memo


Explain the business, the equipment and how it earns its payment, and answer the obvious questions first: a dip in deposits, a late tax filing, an existing lien.


6. 06


Submit complete, then track what comes back


Send the full package to lenders whose criteria the deal fits, and keep a list of every follow-up request so the next file goes out without the same gap.


A few habits help. Get the credit consent and any Form 4506-C signed with the application: the 4506-C lets the lender request the borrower’s tax transcript from the IRS, which releases it only with the taxpayer’s consent.\[4\] For guarantors without a personal financial statement of their own, SBA Form 413 is a free, widely recognized template.\[5\] And keep a running list of what each lender asked for after submission. That list is your next checklist.

## Frequently asked questions


### What documents are required for equipment financing?


It depends on the deal size and the lender. Smaller deals are often application only: a signed application, the equipment quote or invoice and sometimes a few months of business bank statements. Above the lender’s application-only limit, expect business and personal tax returns, year-end and interim financial statements, recent bank statements, a business debt schedule, a personal financial statement for each guarantor, entity documents and, for used or private-party equipment, title and condition details.


### What is an application-only equipment finance deal?


It is a deal the lender decides mainly on the application, the guarantors’ credit, time in business and the equipment, without tax returns or financial statements. Each lender sets its own limit. Several publish limits between $150,000 and $250,000, and the limit can depend on the equipment type and the borrower’s credit. Above it, the lender asks for full financials.


### How many months of bank statements do equipment lenders want?


Three to six recent months is a common request, and some application-only programs ask for three or four. Send every page of every month, downloaded from the bank rather than screenshotted, and make sure the most recent month is actually recent, since a stale statement is one of the most common follow-up requests.


### Why do equipment finance deals stall or get declined?


Many stall on the paperwork before anyone weighs the credit: a missing month or page, a tax return without its schedules, interim statements that are months old, a legal name that differs between the application and the entity documents, or loan payments in the bank statements that are not on the debt schedule. Each gap costs a round trip between lender, broker and borrower, and the equipment quote can expire in the meantime.


### What should a broker’s cover memo include?


A short description of the business and its owners, what the equipment is and how it earns its payment, the requested amount and structure, and an honest answer to anything the analyst will ask about: a dip in deposits, a late tax filing, an existing lien, a recent ownership change. Keep it to a page and let the documents carry the numbers.
